reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because it promotes Ludo-based earning applications with unusually easy cash claims, including earning 1000 rupees every three hours and thousands after depositing money. The speaker repeatedly encourages viewers to try named apps and directs them to referral links and codes, even though he also warns that some other apps are fraudulent.

opening.argument: This is presented as a cautionary comparison, not an unconditional endorsement of every application. The speaker says he will identify which applications viewers should and should not use, and expressly warns viewers not to use an app until its legitimacy is proven. He also labels some applications fake or not legitimate. Those warnings materially qualify the recommendations and show an effort to distinguish safer options from suspected fraud, rather than deceptively presenting all earning claims as reliable.

citations.quote: I'll share with which application you should use and the one you shouldn't use.
Until it is proven scientifically that the app is legit and genuine, don't use the app.
You don't need to try these applications from Unity And this application is totally fake.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The cited earnings statement concerns one application and does not erase the video's repeated warnings about other applications. A recommendation accompanied by a legitimacy qualification is not equivalent to promising that every viewer will profit. The description's referral language shows promotion, but does not by itself establish that the creator concealed risk or guaranteed an outcome.

citations.quote: Until it is proven scientifically that the app is legit and genuine, don't use the app.
application is totally fake.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The warnings are selective, while the speaker still endorses particular applications as legitimate and urges viewers to try them. Saying not to use an app until proven genuine does not substantiate his own positive claims. The video also links installation and referral use to cash rewards, so disclaimers do not remove the solicitation or make the earnings claims reliable.

opening.argument: The video's stated purpose is to review and compare earning applications from a user's perspective. The speaker says he installed applications, tested them, and will explain which ones work and which ones do not. His discussion includes observations about interfaces, withdrawal processes, matching availability, bugs, and automated systems. That is evaluative commentary and user education about app operation, including negative testing of suspected scams, rather than a single-minded demand that viewers pay or participate.

citations.quote: I've installed all their earning applications in my phone.
I'll share with which application you should use and the one you shouldn't use.
its interface is very weak and in many cases the application is buggy.
I tried it myself and saw that there is an automatic system

rebuttal.rebuttal: The existence of criticism does not change the format into a solicitation. The speaker's own description emphasizes testing and comparison, including identifying applications viewers should avoid. References to particular app behavior and withdrawal conditions are precisely the kind of practical information a consumer review would provide, even when the reviewer ultimately recommends some services.

citations.quote: I'll provide this list since I've installed all their earning applications in my phone.
this is simply a scam because it is an automated system

true_side_reply.rebuttal: A review framing cannot neutralize the video's operative recommendations. The speaker says an application is legitimate, reports rapid earnings, and tells viewers to try it; the description supplies referral links and codes. Testing language explains how he arrived at endorsements, but it does not show that the promoted earnings or legitimacy claims were independently established.

opening.argument: The material is consistent with ordinary app promotion and referral rewards surrounding games, not proof of a scam mechanism. The description lists gaming and reward services and gives referral codes, while the spoken content distinguishes applications and discusses user experience. The supplied evidence does not show credential theft, a downline scheme, or a guaranteed return, and it does not establish that installing an app or using a referral code necessarily causes loss. Referral bonuses and app recommendations can exist as ordinary promotions without proving fraud.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The prosecution treats the presence of cash language as proof of a scam, but the evidence also shows a recognizable referral-promotion format and multiple named services. The quoted earnings are the speaker's account, not a statement that every viewer is guaranteed the same result. Most importantly, the cited material does not establish that the promoted apps obtain credentials, operate a downline, or automatically take every participant's deposit.

citations.quote: Install with Referral Code "CNPM4" and get ₹5 rewards.
because I have earned a thousand rupees from it every 3 hours.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Ordinary referral language does not make the central solicitation ordinary. The speaker connects deposits and app participation to substantial claimed withdrawals, and explicitly directs viewers to install through his links and codes. The absence of credential theft or a downline is not decisive because the concern is a low-barrier cash-earning pitch involving installation, deposits, and promised-looking returns.
